a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

claims.claim: Paltusotine, a quinoline-containing basic amine structurally related to the query's quinoline/quinuclidine scaffold, had human absolute oral bioavailability of 69% (90% CI 59-82%) after a 20 mg oral solution versus IV microtracer; L2 records add a separate 70% estimate and describe only a modest capsule-versus-solution reduction.

Moxifloxacin, a methoxy-substituted quinolone bearing a basic bicyclic amine, had human absolute oral bioavailability of approximately 82-92% across studies, with L2 clinical/model estimates of 86-99% and tablet/IV AUC ratios of 0.86-0.998.

Other visible human absolute-bioavailability records are all above the 20% threshold: prasugrel ~79%, GSK1322322 77% fed, veralipride 78.6% capsule and 86.5% solution, zongertinib predicted 41%, and apixaban 37-39% under rifampin induction, with L2 records quantifying the rifampin reduction as about 25%.

L2 records that might appear lower are not threshold-relevant negatives: moxifloxacin rat F was 0.755, and prasugrel active-metabolite relative bioavailability was 25% in rats/dogs, but these are species- or endpoint-specific and remain above 20% or measure a metabolite rather than parent oral F.

The query's physicochemical profile (MW 324, logD 1.29, TPSA 45.6, HBD 1, no Lipinski violations) is consistent with the high-F comparators; the low neutral fraction is not disqualifying given the ionizable basic amines in paltusotine and moxifloxacin.

Transfer from paltusotine and moxifloxacin is based on structural analogy rather than an exact match; the query contains a quinuclidine tertiary amine and a vinyl group not present in those comparators.
Some supporting records are predicted human values or animal values (e.g., zongertinib 41% predicted; prasugrel active metabolite 25% in rats/dogs), limiting direct transferability.
No formulation or food-effect data are available for the query.
